title: Lacing | Clo 2026.0 Features Deep Dive

markdown_content: ## Clo 2026.0 Lacing Feature Overview This section introduces Clo 2026.0’s new **Lacing** feature, where you can generate laces for **garments and shoes**. The feature is located in the **2D toolbar** as a small “lacing” tool. ## Using Lacing on Garments (Layered Unders) This section explains how to place laces through garment layers using the recommended **top-to-bottom traversal** workflow, and how to finish placement with **Enter** so you can still edit the resulting lace. ### Placement Workflow (Start at the Opening, Then Work Down and Back Up) The key tip is to **start from the opening**, work your way **down**, and then go **back up to the other side of the opening**. This is demonstrated on layered garment unders (layer cones/underlayers). In the example: - The user has multiple **layer cone under** sections. - They **do not lace through** the entire set of layers. - Instead, they lace only through the **top layers** (the specific two layers they choose to pass through). - Alternatively, you can lace through the **bottom layers** as well, depending on the desired result. ### Click Sequence in 2D (and Optional 3D) The user places lace points by clicking repeatedly along the opening path. They note: - You can do the process in **3D** as well. - Doing it in **2D** can be easier because clicking can be confusing when layers overlap (especially if you accidentally click the same one twice). Once the lace path is placed: - Press **Enter** to **finish**. - After finishing, the lace can be further edited and adjusted. ## Editing Lace Shape and Curvature (After Placement) This section covers post-placement edits such as **direction (up/down)** and **curvature options**, plus the step that locks the lace placement. ### Change Lace Direction (Flip Up vs Down) After placement, the user adjusts how the lace segment travels: - The first segment can go **down** and then **out/over**, repeatedly. - You can change this by selecting a segment and **flipping** it so it goes **up** (instead of down), effectively switching which part is “top” vs “bottom.” ### Curvature Controls A **curvature** control panel/box labeled **Lacing** provides options to shape how the lace moves, such as: - lace **dropping down** - lace **going up** - or choosing either direction depending on the desired visual. Pressing **Enter** after these adjustments: - sets the lace - makes the lace placement no longer editable as a path - but still allows adjustments to the **fabric lace** pattern piece. ## Fabric Lace Pattern Editing (Width, Length, Fabric Assignment) This section explains how the generated lace becomes a **pattern piece** you can modify, including **width**, **length**, and **fabric material** assignment. ### Modify Lace Pattern Dimensions The lace is created as a pattern piece visible in the model. The user can: - **Change width** (e.g., make the lace thicker) - **Change length** using the **Transform Pattern tool** (the user demonstrates lengthening; they note real measurements can be used) ### Assign Lace Fabric The user applies a specific lace material: - Select the **lace fabric** - Apply it to the created lace pattern piece ## Simulation Setup and Mesh Safety Checks This section describes simulation preparation for lace behavior, emphasizing the importance of **particle distance** and using **wireframe** checks to prevent holes from showing through. ### Particle Distance (Small Particle Distance Recommended) Before **simulate**, the user recommends using a **small particle distance**. In the example: - particle distance values shown include **5** and **10** - the user highlights that smaller distances are preferred ### Wireframe Preview to Detect Poking Through Before running the final simulation: - Use **Show Wire Frame** to check whether holes will **poke through**. The user reports: - The bottom layer has **thin and small mesh**, which they find reassuring. - The top layer also appears likely to be okay. ### Run Simulation After the wireframe check: - Press **simulate** - The lace result is shown as “all set.” ## Handling Simulation Issues (Select Mesh, Pause, Move, Re-Simulate) This section explains a troubleshooting loop when simulation results are not ideal, using **select mesh**, repeated simulation, and moving the lace while respecting collision behavior. ### Troubleshooting Loop If the user expects an issue (they mention they “knew this was going to happen”): 1. Go to **Select Mesh** 2. Select the relevant mesh area 3. Run **simulate** again 4. Repeat as needed: - **Pause simulations** - **Select again** - **Move** the lace/mesh upward - **Simulate** again ### Collision and Mesh Limitations (Important Caveats) The user warns: - **Collision still happens** - Parts can still **poke through** - The mesh might not always behave perfectly - Objects can sometimes go through mesh They recommend moving **slowly** and continuing adjustments to tighten the lace as needed (e.g., shifting/sliding and using interaction controls). ## Using Lacing on Shoes This section explains applying the same Lacing feature to a **shoe**, including how to start placement, handle layered clicking difficulty, adjust curvature, and run simulation. ### Access the Lacing Tool and Start Placement On the shoe: - Return to the **lacing feature** in the **2D toolbar** - Select the lacing tool Placement can be done in **2D** or **3D**: - When layers are stacked, it can be harder to know exactly what you’re clicking. - The user prefers **2D** for precision, but notes **3D** is also usable for editing/playing around. ### Finish Placement The user places the lace path by clicking through the shoe opening area and then presses **Enter** to finish. ### Curvature Adjustment for Shoe Laces The user increases **curvature** so the laces rise higher (“come really high up”). After confirming the lace shape, they press **Enter** and proceed to **simulate**. ### Precision Note They mention: - If you click less precisely (e.g., not flipping/targeting layers perfectly), the result may be harder to refine. - You can stay focused in **3D** if you want to experiment and edit there. ## Simulation for Garments and Shoes This section consolidates the end workflow: after lace placement and edits, run **simulate** to produce the final lace behavior. For both garment and shoe examples: - final lace creation is placed via clicking + **Enter** - you can adjust lace parameters (direction/curvature and fabric/pattern edits) - then run **simulate** to finalize the lacing result
